verses.translation_literal: A psalm of Asaph. Surely [or: Only] good to Israel [is] God, to the pure of heart.
verses.translation_dramatic: A psalm, handed down in the name of Asaph. And it opens in a low, steady voice, the voice of a creed said before the doubt is allowed to speak: Surely God is good to Israel, good to those whose hearts are clean.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the first psalm of Book III, and the words in the title are part of the Hebrew verse, which is why the English verse numbers differ by one: the KJV leaves the superscription as verse 0 and starts counting after it. Asaph was a temple singer, and the line is liturgical: it sounds like the creed a congregation sings. The actor must play it as exactly that, a confession the speaker knows by heart and is about to see tested. Everything after this verse is a story of how it almost failed.

The small word אַךְ is the hinge. The KJV and ASV take it as 'Truly/Surely', an assertion, and Meiri and Radak agree: 'this I know for certain.' But it also carries the sense of 'only' or 'yet', and the psalm lets you hear both: the speaker states the doctrine and then immediately confesses he did not live by it. The KJV smooths the next phrase, 'even to such as are of a clean heart', with an 'even' that is not in the Hebrew; the text says simply 'to Israel, God, to the pure of heart', two parallel phrases. The commentators disagree on what it means: Malbim and Metzudat David read it as a narrowing (God is good only to the inwardly clean among Israel), Ibn Ezra says the same ('not to all of them'), while the Targum says 'to the pure of heart' as an explanation of 'Israel'. It is a striking sequence: the claim is made, and the psalmist will discover that he himself did not qualify.

ברי לבב, 'pure of heart', means one whose inward motives are sifted clean, like grain or silver, not merely innocent of deeds (Metzudat Zion: 'clear and clean of the clouding of sin').

philological_notes.note: A particle that either asserts ('surely', as in Gen 29:14) or restricts ('only', 'yet'). Here it opens a statement the speaker will soon say he almost could not hold, so both senses are live. The Hebrew starts the psalm's argument with this one syllable.

'To the pure of heart'. The word בַּר means clean, sifted, clear; the KJV 'clean' loses the sense of purified through sorting. The heart (לֵבָב) is the seat of thought and will, so the purity is motive and inner life.

verses.translation_literal: And I, like a little [bit], my feet had turned aside, like nothing my steps had been poured out.
verses.translation_dramatic: But I. I came within a breath of it. My feet had turned aside; my footing had all but run out from under me, as water runs out, as if there had never been a path at all.
verses.directors_commentary:
The creed breaks on the word 'I'. The whole psalm now becomes personal, and the actor should drop out of the liturgical tone completely. The two halves of the verse are a matched pair in Hebrew poetry: 'feet turned aside' and 'steps poured out' say the same thing twice, and the doubling is the point; the speaker is shaken. Ibn Ezra notes that the second half simply repeats the first, as in the style of elegant parallelism.

The KJV 'my feet were almost gone; my steps had well nigh slipped' smooths two vivid verbs and replaces them with idiom. The Hebrew says that his feet 'turned aside' (נטה, as one leaves a road) and that his steps were 'poured out' (שפך, the verb for pouring water or blood). The picture is of a path that liquefies. Meiri and Radak note that the written text (Ketiv) has 'bent' in the singular and 'poured' in the feminine singular, which suggests each foot being bent and tripping, while the reading tradition (Qere) makes both plural. In the ancient world, feet and walking are the ordinary image for moral and religious life (the 'way' of God), so 'my feet nearly turned' means 'I nearly abandoned the faith'. Rashi says directly: 'to turn away from after God.'

The two מעט and אין phrases ('like a little', 'like nothing') both measure how narrow the escape was.

philological_notes.note: 'My steps': the placing of the foot in a walk, from the root 'to go straight, to step'. Metzudat Zion links it with Psalm 37:31 ('his steps do not slip'). The picture is of footprints dissolving.
'Were poured out': the verb for water or blood. The Ketiv שפכה is singular and the Qere שפכו is plural, a difference Radak and Meiri comment on.

verses.translation_literal: For I was jealous at the boasters; the peace of wicked ones I saw.
verses.translation_dramatic: For I was jealous. I envied the loud ones, the boasters, when I looked and saw how peaceful the wicked were.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the cause of the stumble is given, and it is not a theory but an emotion: קנאה, jealousy, the same word used for a man's jealousy over his wife and for God's own zeal. The actor should not play this as a philosopher's puzzle. It is the raw, private feeling of someone who has done the right thing and watches the wrong ones thrive.

The KJV calls them 'the foolish' and the ASV 'the arrogant'. The Hebrew הוללים comes from the root הלל, which means to boast, to make a noise, and also to rave like a madman (Metzudat Zion links it to folly, 'a spirit of foolishness enters a man who sins'). Ibn Ezra takes it as the active form of 'those who praise themselves'. Rashi gives a different sense, 'mixers, confusers', and compares it to wine mixed with water. The KJV 'foolish' is a fair rendering of one strand, but it drops the noise of a boaster. And שלום, the word the KJV renders 'prosperity', is the full Hebrew word for peace and well-being, which is why the speaker's jealousy is so painful: they have the thing the faithful are promised.

The verb 'I saw' (אראה) is in the imperfect: it describes something he kept seeing, not a single glance.

philological_notes.note: From הלל 'to boast, rave', so 'boasters, braggarts' and also 'the mad, the foolish'. The same root gives 'praise' (hallel), a reminder that boasting is praise turned onto oneself.
Not just 'prosperity' (KJV) but peace, wholeness, being unharmed. The speaker envies their security, not only their wealth.

verses.translation_literal: For there are no bonds to their death, and fat [is] their body [or: sound their porch].
verses.translation_dramatic: For death itself holds no terrors for them: no pangs, no struggle at the end. Their bodies are sleek and sound.
verses.directors_commentary:
The wicked's secure life is described physically. There is a problem in this verse that every translator hits: חרצבות occurs elsewhere only in Isaiah 58:6 ('loose the bonds of wickedness'), where it means bonds or knots. Rashi, Radak and Meiri all read it that way here: death for the wicked is not a struggle against ties, they die easily. The KJV 'no bands in their death' keeps that, while the ASV 'pangs' gives a looser sense. Rashi also records a rabbinic notarikon (a playful reading of the letters) that makes it 'they are not anxious and sad about the day of death.' The whole line says that these people do not even suffer at the end.

The second half is harder. בריא means fat, healthy, plump (the same word is used of well-fed cattle), and אולם is unclear: 'their body', 'their strength' (from 'there is power in my hand'; Ibn Ezra and Radak), or 'their hall/porch' (Ibn Ezra, Metzudat Zion). The KJV 'their strength is firm' and BBE 'their bodies are fat and strong' both guess. For a modern audience the relevant fact is that in a world where most people were thin from labour and famine and died young of illness, being fat meant wealth and power, and a quiet death was rare. That is why this verse hurts.

philological_notes.note: A rare noun meaning 'bonds, pangs, knots'. Its only other occurrence is Isaiah 58:6. Rashi, Meiri and Metzudat Zion all connect the two places.
Disputed: 'body', 'strength' (Ibn Ezra, Radak), or 'porch, hall' (Metzudat Zion calls it 'a palace'). Elsewhere אולם means the porch of a temple or house.

verses.translation_literal: In the toil of humankind they are not, and with humankind they are not stricken.
verses.translation_dramatic: They do not labour as the rest of humanity labours. The blows that fall on other people never land on them.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse is a mirror structure: 'in the toil of mankind they are not' and 'with mankind they are not stricken'. The Hebrew uses two different words for humanity here, אנוש (the frail, mortal one) and אדם (the human), and the English versions usually turn both into 'other men' or 'men', which hides the point that the speaker puts these people outside the shared lot of mortals. The KJV 'as other men' is not in the Hebrew; there is no 'as'. They are simply not in the toil. The speaker is saying that the curse of Genesis 3, work by sweat and the ordinary blows of life, bypasses them.

The word עמל means toil and trouble, labour that exhausts. The verb ינגעו comes from נגע, 'to touch, strike', the verb used for the plague-marks of skin disease and for God's blows. Radak says it means that when sickness comes to others, it does not come to them. Ibn Ezra adds that this is because they are rich: money buys them out of toil. The Targum, interestingly, rewrites the verse entirely to say that the wicked have no part in the toil of the scholars.

philological_notes.note: Toil, labour and the trouble it brings. A key word in Ecclesiastes. Here it is the common human burden the wicked escape.
'They are struck, plagued': the verb of the divine blow (the nega' of Leviticus). It makes the speaker's complaint sharper: the very blows God sends do not reach them.

verses.translation_literal: Therefore pride [is] a necklace for them; a garment of violence covers [them], for them.
verses.translation_dramatic: And so pride is the chain they wear at the throat, and violence is the robe they wrap around themselves, and wear as if it were theirs by right.
verses.directors_commentary:
From here the speaker turns from what the wicked lack to what they wear. The image is of jewellery and clothing, the visible signs of rank. ענק is a neck ornament, a collar or chain (it is the word behind the Anakim, 'long-necked' giants, and Prov 1:9 uses it of the ornament that wisdom is to the neck). Pride is not an inner feeling here; it is an item of dress they put on, which every onlooker can see. Rashi adds a coarse note: the violence they do makes them fat, so that the garment of violence covers their very flesh.

The KJV has 'compasseth them about as a chain', which captures the necklace but not the fact that the necklace is, in the Hebrew, the pride itself, with no 'as'. The second half has a difficulty: שית is a very rare word. STEPBible and the KJV take it as 'garment' (the sense follows from the verb 'wrap'). Meiri reads it as 'foundation' (as in Isa 19:10), and Ibn Ezra offers 'way' or 'side'. Whichever it is, the structure is a matched pair: pride as ornament, violence as clothing. The final 'for them' (למו) is an old poetic form of 'to them' and appears twice in these verses; it stresses ownership.

Note also the stress of the verb 'covers' (יעטף), which is a verb for wrapping oneself, as of a cloak around the shoulders; the picture is of someone who wears violence with ease.

philological_notes.note: A verb made from the noun ענק 'neck ornament': 'it necklaced them'. The pride becomes a collar they wear. Metzudat David and Zion both read it as a chain that goes around the neck.
An unclear rare word, translated 'garment' by most English versions. Meiri takes it as 'foundation', Ibn Ezra as 'way, side'. I follow the 'garment' reading, which suits the verb 'wraps'.

token_glosses.gloss: it is a necklace for them

verses.translation_literal: It goes out from fat, their eyes; they pass over, the imaginings of [the] heart.
verses.translation_dramatic: Their eyes swell out of faces gone heavy with fat, bulging as if the flesh could hardly hold them. And their hearts? Whatever the heart could picture, whatever it dared to want, they have already passed it by, and gone on beyond.
verses.directors_commentary:
Play the first half as physical comedy turned sour. The Hebrew says the eyes 'go out from fat', and Rashi and Radak picture eyes that bulge, or vanish, in a face padded with fat. In a world where most people were lean, and bread was never certain, a fat face was a statement of wealth, and also of appetite that has no limit. Meiri disagrees: he thinks it means that their colour and gleam 'go out' like shine, and he says fat does not make eyes bulge, so the reading is open. Keep the physical one for the stage.

The second half is harder. 'Pass over the imaginings of the heart' means that reality has gone beyond even what their minds could invent: they get more than they dreamed of. The KJV 'more than heart could wish' is a good guess at the sense, and softens an odd verb, 'pass over', that carries the sense of crossing a boundary. The ASV says the same. The YLT, 'the imaginations of the heart transgressed', is closer to the Hebrew and deliberately strange. Note that the verb is plural and the first verb is singular. The Hebrew is rough here, and the actor should let it stay rough.

philological_notes.note: Rare. Ibn Ezra (quoting R. Moshe) and Radak derive it from שֶׂכְוִי 'mind, heart' (Job 38:36), so 'what the mind envisions'. Ibn Ezra's alternative links it with מַשְׂכִּית, 'carved figure' (the 'figured stone'), so the images the heart carves for itself.
'Fat', and also 'the best part'. The word works on both senses: the fat of the body and the finest of everything. The wicked have both.

verses.translation_literal: They mock and speak with evil, oppression; from on high they speak.
verses.translation_dramatic: They jeer, and the jeering drips from their mouths like poison. They speak of crushing the weak as if it were small talk, and they say it from a height, from a place where no one can answer.
verses.directors_commentary:
The first verb, ימיקו, appears nowhere else in the Bible, and the commentators do not agree on it. Radak and Meiri take it as 'they dissolve, they melt others with their words', a root that means to waste away. Meiri says it is a different root from 'they waste away in their iniquity' (Lev 26:39), and Ibn Ezra compares 'his flesh will rot' (Zech 14:12, המק בשרו). Rashi simply says they do it 'to their neighbours'. So the speakers act like men who rot others with their talk. The KJV 'they are corrupt' softens an action into a state, and the ASV 'they scoff' is nearer to the sense.

The last phrase, 'from on high they speak', is both a posture and a claim. Rashi names Pharaoh ('Who is the LORD that I should obey?'), Sennacherib and Nebuchadnezzar: kings who talked as if no god stood above them. Radak and Ibn Ezra read it as 'there is no one on high above them'. They speak from an elevated seat, that is, with the confidence of power, and Meiri says openly and without shame. The KJV 'loftily' is correct but pale. For the stage, give them a physical height, a throne or a platform, and let the voice come down.

philological_notes.note: A hapax, from a hollow root. The old commentators relate it to 'melt, rot': Radak and Metzudat Zion say 'from melting and dissolving'. Meiri separates it from ימקו (Lev 26:39, root מקק); Ibn Ezra relates it to Zech 14:12. Because the sense is inferred, 'mock' is a hypothesis.
Extortion, the use of power to take from those who cannot resist. Rashi: 'to oppress the poor'. In the prophets it is the typical sin of the powerful against the weak.

verses.translation_literal: They have set in the heavens their mouth, and their tongue walks on the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: They have set their mouths in the very heavens, and their tongues go striding over the earth.
verses.directors_commentary:
The image is a mouth planted in the sky and a tongue that walks. The text does not say 'against' the heavens: the KJV adds that word, and it is one reading (Meiri: to speak evil of God and say His knowledge does not reach below), but the Hebrew is the simple 'in the heavens'. The mouth sits where God sits, and the tongue goes where people live. It is a picture of reach, as though they have claimed both realms, the divine and the human.

The verb 'walks' is feminine, agreeing with the feminine noun 'tongue', and walking is the verb for a person taking a stroll, not for speech. Ibn Ezra reads the tongue as a spy 'going about the land to collect gossip'. Metzudat David adds that, though the tongue is under heaven, they dare to speak to Him who sits in it. The doubled consonant in שתו is, as Radak and Ibn Ezra say, a sign of the root שתת, 'to set, place', not the more common שית. A modern reader would hear: nothing is off limits to their speech, neither God nor neighbour.

philological_notes.note: 'They set', from the root שתת (as Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri note, a doubled form that stands for שיתו). The KJV's 'against' interprets the setting as hostile, which the Hebrew leaves open.
'Walks': a picture of the tongue as a walker who strolls through the land. Ibn Ezra takes it to be like a spy.

verses.translation_literal: Therefore his people returns [or: turns back] hither, and waters of fullness are drained by them.
verses.translation_dramatic: And so his own people turn back and come here, and drink what is poured out for them, the water of a full cup, drained to the last drop.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is among the hardest verses in the Psalter, and a director should say so to the actors: nobody is sure who is doing what. 'His people' (עמו) may be God's people, who see the wicked thrive and come back to their side (Rashi), or who return again and again in bewilderment (Radak, Meiri), or the people of the wicked man. The word הלם, 'here, hither', is equally unclear; Rashi and Metzudat Zion take it as a simple 'here' (compare Judg 18:3, Exod 3:5), Radak as 'in this matter, this argument'.

The verb has two readings: the written text (Ketiv) says ישיב, 'he brings back, he turns', and the reading tradition (Qere) says ישוב, 'he returns'. In the first, God Himself brings his people to this puzzle (Radak, Meiri). 'Waters of a full [cup]' is clearly missing a noun: Ibn Ezra supplies 'cup', Radak 'a cup of poison', and Meiri compares the construction to Habakkuk 1:16. Then 'drained' (ימצו) is the verb for sucking or wringing out, as of a fleece. The KJV 'wrung out' and ASV 'drained' have both preserved the squeezing, but the BBE has abandoned the verse's meaning altogether ('they are full of bread').

I render the Hebrew as it stands and do not choose: the people are drawn, and what is drained for them is full to the brim, whether as bitterness (Radak, Meiri), as wine of prosperity, or as the water of teaching they now treat as nothing (Rashi).

philological_notes.note: 'Hither, here'. Rashi cites Judg 18:3 and Metzudat Zion Exod 3:5. Radak reads it as 'in this matter'.
'They are drained, wrung out': the verb of squeezing or sucking out (Metzudat Zion links it to מציצה, sucking).

verses.translation_literal: And they say, How does God know? And is there knowledge in the Most High?
verses.translation_dramatic: And they say, How could God know? Is there any knowing in the Most High at all?
verses.directors_commentary:
The taunt is a double question, the second repeating the first in a higher name: 'El', God, and then 'Elyon', the Most High. Doubling in this way is a standard feature of Hebrew poetry, and Meiri and Metzudat David say that is what the second half does. The KJV's rendering is accurate in form, but the sound of the Hebrew is more cutting: אֵיכָה, 'how?', is the word of mockery and of lament (it is the opening word of the book of Lamentations), and it is easy to play it as a sneer.

Who says it? The verse names no subject, only 'and they say'. Rashi, Radak and Meiri understand the speakers to be the wicked, or the bewildered of God's own people. Ibn Ezra, alone, thinks the speakers are God's people, citing the next verse 'behold, these are wicked': in his reading the faithful are the ones who say, 'how does God know?' while looking at the wicked. The actor should decide how much of the doubt belongs to the speaker himself. In the context of the psalm the answer is: more than he would like to admit.

The divine names are old ones. אֵל is the ancient Semitic word for god, and עֶלְיוֹן, 'Most High', was a title also used in Canaan; the speakers take God's rank as the reason to doubt that He bothers to look.

philological_notes.note: 'How?', a word of mockery or of lament. It is the first word of the book of Lamentations. Here it is rhetorical: 'how could He possibly know?'
'Knowledge', a rare noun (also Isa 11:9). The question is whether the Most High has awareness of human conduct at all.

verses.translation_literal: Behold, these [are] wicked ones, and always at ease, they have increased wealth.
verses.translation_dramatic: Look at them. These are the wicked. Always at ease, always gathering, and their wealth only grows.
verses.directors_commentary:
The first section of the psalm ends on a pointing finger: 'Behold, these!' The actor should say it as the speaker's raw exhibit, evidence in an argument he is losing with himself. The verse is a flat statement of three things, 'wicked', 'at ease', 'rich', and it is the sum of the complaint.

The KJV calls them 'the ungodly, who prosper in the world'. The Hebrew word is the same רשעים used in verse 3, 'wicked ones', and the translation 'ungodly' is a theological softening of a word that means those who are in the wrong with respect to others as well as with God. The phrase שלוי עולם could mean 'at ease for ever' (ASV, BBE: 'always at ease') or 'at ease in the world' (KJV), and the commentators split in the same way: Rashi, Radak and Metzudat David read it as 'at ease in this world, lifelong'. The verb השגו is 'they increase' (it is the same verb as a cedar that 'grows tall', Psalm 92:13: Metzudat Zion), and חיל, 'wealth', also means strength and army, so the word can carry both power and money. The KJV 'riches' is correct for the sense of resources, but a Hebrew listener would also hear 'might'.

philological_notes.note: 'At ease of perpetuity': carefree for ever, or carefree in this world. The adjective שלו means untroubled, complacent; it suggests security that has lost fear of consequence.
'Wealth', also 'strength, power, army'. Metzudat Zion cites Psalm 62:11 for the sense 'wealth'.

verses.translation_literal: Surely for nothing I have kept pure my heart, and I washed in innocence my palms.
verses.translation_dramatic: And I? I kept my heart clean, and for what? For nothing. I washed my hands in innocence, and the water ran off them into the dust, and it bought me nothing at all.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the low point of the confession, and it should be played quietly, not shouted: a decent man doing the sums and finding they do not add up. Two body parts carry the claim, heart for inner life and palms for deeds, and Ibn Ezra notes that most actions are done with the hands. The washing of hands in innocence is a ritual gesture as well as a figure: Deuteronomy 21:6 has the elders wash their hands to clear a city of blood-guilt, and Psalm 26:6 uses the same image at the altar. Priests and worshippers washed before approaching the sanctuary, so the speaker is saying that his devotion was a practice, not a mood, and that the practice has failed him.

KJV 'in vain' is accurate, and 'cleansed' is acceptable for זִכִּיתִי, but it flattens the little drumbeat of אַךְ ('surely, only') at the start; the Hebrew opens with a bitter sigh and the word 'for nothing' (רִיק) follows at once. It is the same 'surely' that opened the psalm in verse 1 ('Surely God is good'), now turned on itself. BBE's 'made clean to no purpose' is closer to the sense than YLT's 'a vain thing'.

philological_notes.note: 'Surely/only' plus 'emptily'. The word אַךְ echoes the opening of the psalm ('Surely God is good', v.1) and returns in v.18; here it is the cry of disappointment, there it is the verdict of understanding. רִיק is an adverbial 'for nothing'.
Piel: 'I have made pure, kept clean'. The verb is about purity of substance, like clean water, not about legal acquittal.

verses.translation_literal: And I have been stricken all the day, and my rebuke at the mornings.
verses.translation_dramatic: All day long the blows fall on me. And morning after morning, before I am even awake, the correction is waiting at my door.
verses.directors_commentary:
The two halves of the verse are a clock: 'all the day' and 'at the mornings', that is, every day from dawn to dusk. The speaker feels that suffering is an appointment he keeps. For the original audience, נָגוּעַ ('stricken', from נגע, touch or strike) was the word for the plague and the skin disease of Leviticus 13, so it sounds like an affliction sent by God, not misfortune. תוֹכַחְתִּי ('my rebuke') is the word of the wisdom teacher who corrects a son (Prov 3:11-12); the speaker is saying that he is disciplined like a disobedient child while the wicked, who really deserve it, are never touched (v.5).

KJV 'plagued' and 'chastened' have the right sense, but the dawn imagery is lost: the Hebrew has a plural 'mornings', so the beat is each new dawn, which Rashi reads as new troubles every morning. Radak and Meiri both explain it as the ongoing suffering at the hands of the wicked; Ibn Ezra adds a second reading, in which the 'rebuke' is the speaker's own, directed at himself, but the natural reading is that it is God's correction.

philological_notes.note: Passive participle, 'one struck, afflicted'. The root gives נֶגַע, the 'plague-mark' of Leviticus 13, so the word has the sound of an affliction from God.
Plural 'to the mornings', that is, 'every morning' (Ibn Ezra compares 'new every morning', Lam 3:23).

verses.translation_literal: If I had said, I will recount like them, behold, the generation of your sons I would have betrayed.
verses.translation_dramatic: If I had said it out loud, if I had told it the way they tell it, then look: I would have betrayed your children, the whole generation of them.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker has just voiced a thought that shakes his faith, and now he pulls back. He is not silent from fear of God but from responsibility for others: if he spoke the doubt aloud, the 'generation of your sons', the ordinary believers who look to him, would hear it and be lost. Play it as a hand across the mouth. The word בָּגַד is the language of treason and marriage-breaking (Jer 3:20, Mal 2:14), so the speaker casts his own possible speech as a betrayal of the family of God.

The verse is hard and the commentators struggle with it. Radak and Meiri say the word הִנֵּה is displaced, so that it reads 'if I said I will speak as they do, I would have betrayed', and Rashi takes it as the speaker's thought of speaking everything as it is. KJV 'I should offend against' is too mild: the Hebrew is treachery, not offence. 'Thy children' is also slightly off, since בָּנִים are sons, the term for the people as God's family (Deut 14:1). BBE turns the verse into a charge against God, which has no support in the Hebrew, where the speaker is the possible traitor.

philological_notes.note: 'I would have acted treacherously'. The perfect here is conditional ('I would have betrayed'). The root is used of faithless spouses and covenant breakers.
'I will recount like them'. The final word is the poetic form of כְּ, 'like', with the object left to the reader: like the wicked who say 'How does God know?' (v.11), as Meiri supplies.

verses.translation_literal: And I thought to know this; toil it was in my eyes.
verses.translation_dramatic: So I turned it over in my mind, trying to understand. And all I found was labor. It wore my eyes out.
verses.directors_commentary:
From here the psalm turns inward: the speaker tries to think his way out and fails. עָמָל is the word for hard labor and grinding trouble, the word of Ecclesiastes ('toil under the sun'), so the problem is not only unanswered but exhausting, and 'in my eyes' places the strain in the very act of looking. The Hebrew is blunt where KJV 'too painful for me' paraphrases: there is no 'too', and nothing says 'painful'; it says simply 'it was toil'. Rashi gives a different sense, taking it as 'this seemed to me a wearying thing and not justice', but the verse itself has only 'trouble'.

The written text (Ketiv) has הִיא, 'she', where the reader says הוּא, 'he'; Radak and Meiri discuss this and agree that the sense is the same ('it was toil'). The speaker's silence is not peace, it is effort.

philological_notes.note: Labor, trouble, the weariness of a task that does not end. A favorite word of Ecclesiastes. Here it is the effort of thinking, not injustice; Rashi, who reads the verse as a charge against God's way, is reading further than the Hebrew goes.
The Ketiv is הִיא, the Qere הוּא; both mean 'it' here, and the Masoretic note is only about the spelling.

verses.translation_literal: Until I came into the sanctuaries of God, I understood their end.
verses.translation_dramatic: Until I went in, into the holy places of God. And there, there I saw it. I understood how they end.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the pivot of the whole psalm, and the director should give it a long silence before 'until'. Everything before it is argument and fatigue; everything after is sight. The speaker does not say what he found in the temple: no vision, no oracle, no sermon. Whatever he learned, he learned in the place where God is present, by standing in worship, and what changed was his view of 'their end', the אַחֲרִית, which can mean the final outcome of a life, or what is left afterward (Prov 23:18, 24:14).

KJV has the plural 'sanctuary' in the singular; the Hebrew has מִקְדְּשֵׁי, 'holy places', a plural of fullness that covers the whole holy precinct, as in Psalm 68:36. The tense is also a trap: אָבוֹא is a verb of the imperfect form ('I will go in'), and the sense is 'until I would come in', as Ibn Ezra notes, so the experience is told from within. The commentators split on what happened there: Rashi says the speaker saw Sennacherib's army fall; Radak and Malbim take it as a vision of the world to come; Metzudat David says he consulted the priests who taught there; Meiri says it is a figure of understanding.

philological_notes.note: 'Sanctuaries of God': a plural form of the noun for 'holy place'. It may mean the temple with its courts and chambers, or any place of presence.
'To/for their end', literally 'their after-part'. It means the final outcome, as in Proverbs 14:12 and 23:18.

verses.translation_literal: Surely, on slippery [places] you set them; you made them fall to ruins.
verses.translation_dramatic: But the ground you gave them was glass. You set them down on it yourself, and now, with one push, you throw them down, you bring them down into the ruin they never saw coming.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the turn of the psalm, and it begins with a short, hard 'Surely' (אַךְ), the same word the speaker used in verse 13 for 'surely in vain'. Then it was a complaint; now it is a discovery. Play it as the moment when something clicks, in a place of worship: the same prosperity that looked like a reward is the road to the fall.

The image is of a smooth path: Radak and Meiri picture a man walking on a polished, easy road, who suddenly slips and falls. Rashi and Metzudat David add that the good things that come to them are only payment for the little good they did, so the road is paved. The subject is God, 'you set, you made fall', and the second person speaks to God directly for the first time.

The KJV 'thou castedst them down' is archaic but accurate, since the Hebrew hiphil is causative: God himself brings them down. The ASV 'thou castest' is smoother. 'Into destruction' is the traditional rendering of משואות, a plural of שׁוֹאָה: ruins, desolations, and Metzudat Zion links it with the 'desolate wasteland' of Job 30:3. Ibn Ezra reports that some derive it instead from the verb of 'the serpent deceived me' (Gen 3:13), so 'deceptions', and he calls that meaning 'doubled' with the other. STEPBible follows that reading. The sense is probably both: they were deceived, and they fell into ruin.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil, 'you made them fall', causative, with the suffix 'them'. God is the actor, not just a bystander as 'let them fall' would suggest.

Usually 'ruins, desolations' (from שׁוֹאָה, cf. Job 30:3 as Metzudat Zion cites it). Ibn Ezra reports an opinion from נשא 'to deceive' (Gen 3:13, 'the serpent deceived me'), which is the source of the gloss 'deceptions'.

verses.translation_literal: How they have become a waste, like a moment! They have come to an end, they are finished, from sudden terrors.
verses.translation_dramatic: How quickly it happens. One moment, and they are a desolation. They are gone, finished, swept away by terror.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker gasps; this is the sight of the fall. 'How!' (אֵיךְ) is the cry of the lament and the funeral song (2 Sam 1:19, Lam 1:1), here directed at the sudden collapse of people who had seemed untouchable. 'Like a moment' (כְרָגַע) is the whole sermon in one word: the long prosperity of the wicked is a blink beside what follows. The verse stacks synonyms, 'come to an end, are finished', with the hammering rhythm of a verdict.

KJV 'brought into desolation' and 'consumed with terrors' are accurate but soften בַּלָּהוֹת, the 'sudden terrors' that come on the wicked in Job 18:11 and 18:14, where Terror is nearly a person, the 'king of terrors'. Rashi reads them as demons (שֵׁדִים), and Metzudat Zion notes the word is a reversal of בהלות, panic. The audience would hear a fear that strikes before the victim can prepare.

philological_notes.note: 'Sudden terrors', from the root of panic. In Job 18:11, 14 and 27:20 they chase the wicked; Rashi glosses them as demons, Metzudat Zion as an inversion of בהלות 'panic'.
'They have come to an end', from the root that gives סוֹף, 'end'.

token_glosses.gloss: they have come to an end

verses.translation_literal: Like a dream from [one] waking, O Lord, in rousing, their image you will despise.
verses.translation_dramatic: Like a dream when the sleeper wakes, and is gone before the eyes are open. So, Lord, when you rise and stir, you will look at what they were, their image, their shape, and you will hold it worthless.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse is built on two different verbs of waking. First the human one, הקיץ (the sleeper surfacing), then the divine one, בעיר, from the root עור, ‘to rouse, to stir’. The sound of the second half echoes the first: the verse is one long waking. Do not let the actor play the Lord as a man shaken from sleep; the poem has just said that the wicked are swept away in a moment (v. 19), and this is the same moment seen from the other side. Their prosperity was only ever dream-stuff: the speaker took it for solid because he was inside the dream.

Two words are not settled. בעיר can be read ‘in the city’ (Rashi: Jerusalem, where they were disgraced; Meiri: the city where they paraded their wealth) or as ‘in rousing’ (Radak; the Targum takes it as the rousing of the dead at the great day). The Hebrew allows both, and the speaker may well want the echo. צלם is the ‘image’ in Gen 1:26, a shape or likeness, not the thing: the ancient ear hears an idol-like figure with nothing inside it. תבזה is ‘hold in contempt’, a stronger word than the KJV’s ‘despise’ may sound today, though the sense is the same. The KJV’s ‘so’ and its two ‘thou’s are added; the Hebrew simply sets the dream and the Lord side by side with no connecting word.

philological_notes.note: ‘From the waking’, the human waking, from sleep. It is a different root from בעיר, so the verse does not repeat one verb; it pairs two. The pairing makes the Lord’s act the counterpart of the sleeper’s.
Parsed here as bĕ + infinitive of עור, ‘in rousing’, with the Lord as subject. The same consonants read as ‘in the city’; Rashi and Meiri take it so, Radak and the Targum take it as rousing.
‘Their image’: the shape or likeness without substance. Radak lets it mean body, spirit or both.

verses.translation_literal: For my heart was soured, and in my kidneys I was pierced.
verses.translation_dramatic: My heart went sour in me. And I was stabbed in the deepest part of myself, in the kidneys, where a man feels everything.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker looks back at himself, and the language is physical. יִתְחַמֵּץ is 'it turned sour', from the word for leaven and vinegar (חָמֵץ), the sourness of fermenting bread and wine: his heart soured like wine left too long. אֶשְׁתּוֹנָן is 'I was sharpened, pierced', from the root of the sharp arrow (Ps 45:6) and the sharpened tooth, so the bitterness was an inner wound.

The kidneys (כְּלָיוֹת) are the seat of the deepest feelings and of conscience in Hebrew: God 'tests heart and kidneys' (Ps 7:10). KJV renders them 'reins', an old word for kidneys, which is correct but obscure, and 'grieved' for יִתְחַמֵּץ loses the sourness; ASV's 'soul' and 'heart' mixes the organs. Rashi and Metzudat Zion connect the verb to vinegar and anger; Radak reads it as a sour state of mind with nothing sweet to rest on. The tense is imperfect, so the soured heart was a continuing condition.

philological_notes.note: Hithpael: 'it turned sour', 'was embittered'. From the root of leaven and vinegar. Metzudat Zion says the metaphor stands for anger.
'My kidneys'. In Hebrew psychology the kidneys are the seat of the inner life and moral sense (Ps 7:10, 16:7, Jer 12:2). Meiri adds the rabbinic idea of kidneys as counselors.
Hithpolel from שָׁנַן, 'sharpen, pierce'. Rashi cites 'a sharp sword' (Prov 25:18); Radak and Ibn Ezra connect it to 'a sharp arrow'.

verses.translation_literal: And I was stupid and did not know; beasts I was with you.
verses.translation_dramatic: And I was stupid. I understood nothing. Like an animal I stood before you, dumb and blind.
verses.directors_commentary:
The great confession is here: the speaker turns his anger on himself. בַּעַר is the one who is dull, who is, literally, 'like cattle'; the root appears in 'brutish' in Proverbs 12:1 ('he who hates reproof is בַּעַר'), so it is a hard word, the word for someone who will not learn. Then he calls himself 'beasts' (בְּהֵמוֹת), a plural: a plural of intensity, 'a great beast' (as in Job 40:15, Behemoth), so he is a beast of beasts, and the verb is singular 'I was'.

KJV 'as a beast before thee' adds 'as' and 'before'; the Hebrew says 'I was beasts with you', without a simile, and עִמָּךְ is closeness: with you. He stood next to God without understanding, as a draft animal stands next to its master. Radak reads 'with you' as 'in serving you', since he did not know whether there is reward at all; Metzudat David reads it as 'in your governance'. Notice the reversal: in v.2-3 he envied those who live as if for pleasure, and now he has described himself with an animal word.

philological_notes.note: 'Dull, brutish, stupid': the word is built on the root for 'beast, cattle'. It marks the person who has the capacity to learn and refuses it (Prov 12:1, Ps 92:7).
Plural of בְּהֵמָה 'animal'. Here an intensive plural, 'a great beast'; the same form names the monster Behemoth in Job 40:15.

verses.translation_literal: And I [am] continually with you; you have taken hold of my right hand.
verses.translation_dramatic: And yet I was never away from you. All the time I was at your side, and you held me. You had my right hand in yours.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood changes completely with 'and I': after the sourness and the shame, a sudden tenderness. The speaker was an animal and he was still held. The picture is of a father leading a child by the hand, or of God holding the right hand of a king (Isa 41:13, 45:1); the right hand is the strong hand, the one that would pull away, so for God to take it means the speaker did not hold on to God, God held on to him. The point is that his faithfulness was not his own achievement.

KJV 'Nevertheless' invents a contrast that the Hebrew simply states with 'and'; the phrase 'I am continually with you' echoes 'beasts I was with you' of the previous verse, the same preposition עִמָּךְ in the same place in the line, so the beast who was with God is the same man who is always with God. Rashi and Ibn Ezra link the grip on the right hand with the speaker's feet that 'nearly turned aside' (v.2): God held him when he slipped. The Malbim reads the two hands as the two parts of a person, which goes well beyond the text.

philological_notes.note: 'You have seized the hand of my right': a firm grip, as of a parent on a child about to fall. Rashi and Ibn Ezra tie it to v.2 ('my feet had almost slipped').
'Continually', the word used for the 'perpetual' offering in the temple (the tamid). The speaker's life is a standing presence before God.

verses.translation_literal: In your counsel you guide me, and after, [to] honor you will take me.
verses.translation_dramatic: By your counsel you lead me, step by step, and I am led. And afterward, into honor, you will take me.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker has just said that God holds his right hand (v. 23). Here the hand leads. בעצתך is ‘in your counsel’, and the picture is of someone walked along a road by a guide who knows it; the verb תנחני is the shepherd’s and the desert guide’s verb. The second half is the hard one, and the accents help. A pause is marked after אחר, so ‘and after’ stands a little apart from כבוד. That supports the KJV’s ‘afterward … to glory’: Rashi reads it as ‘afterward, to honor you will take me’, supplying the preposition ל, and Radak likewise says אחר is not joined to כבוד. The KJV’s only addition is that ‘to’; the Hebrew has the bare word ‘honor’.

Other readings are old and serious. Ibn Ezra offers ‘after this honor you will take me’, or ‘after, you will take me, and I [am] honor, like one of the angels’. Radak takes כבודי, ‘my honor’, as the soul, so that ‘you take’ is the soul’s gathering to God at death. Rashi also records what the verse would mean if the accent fell on כבוד, tying it to Sennacherib. The verb לקח, ‘take’, is used elsewhere for Enoch (Gen 5:24), and Ibn Ezra draws that parallel. The text does not say where; keep the actor’s line open, hopeful and not geographical.

philological_notes.note: ‘And after, honor’. The accent marks a pause after אחר, which supports ‘afterward, [to] honor’ (Rashi, Radak) with an implied preposition. Ibn Ezra reads ‘after this honor, take me’; Radak reads ‘take my honor’, the soul. Each is a possible reading of the same four letters.
‘You will take me’. The same verb as for Enoch’s being taken (Gen 5:24); Ibn Ezra makes that link. It does not say where.

verses.translation_literal: Who [is] to me in the heavens? And with you I have not delighted on the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: Who is there for me in heaven? Who? And beside you, on all this earth, there is nothing my heart has wanted.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker is still talking to God, as he has since v. 18, and this question needs no pause from the actor: it is spoken to the one he is sure is listening. The first line is a question, מי לי בשמים, ‘who is mine in the heavens?’, and the implied answer is ‘no one but you’. Rashi spells it out (‘did I choose some angel as my god? I chose only you’) and the Targum adds ‘except you’. The Hebrew itself has no ‘but’ and no ‘beside’; the KJV’s ‘but thee’ and ‘beside thee’ are supplied, and the second line has only ‘and with you’. Ibn Ezra reports a reading that supplies זולתך, ‘other than you’, after ‘in the heavens’.

For an ancient hearer, ‘the heavens’ meant the host of powers worshipped across the region: sun, moon and stars were gods in Mesopotamia and Canaan. Radak hears polemic: some believe in the sun or a star, some worship the four elements, and I set no partner by you in heaven or on earth. The verb חפצתי is ‘take pleasure’, ‘delight’: the point is wanting, not owning. The KJV’s ‘desire’ is close.

philological_notes.note: ‘Who [is] to me in the heavens?’ The Hebrew has no ‘but you’. The implied answer is ‘no one but you’ (Rashi, the Targum). Ibn Ezra cites a reading that supplies זולתך.
‘I took pleasure, I desired’. The perfect states a settled disposition, ‘I have not delighted’.

verses.translation_literal: Finished is my flesh and my heart; rock of my heart and my portion [is] God, for ever.
verses.translation_dramatic: My flesh is failing, and my heart with it. But God is the rock beneath my heart, and my portion, God, for ever and for all time.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker's body gives way in the first half and a rock appears in the second, so let the voice drop and then rise on 'rock'. The verse has two body words: sha'eri ('my flesh', often kin or close flesh) and levavi ('my heart', the seat of mind and will, which Hebrew places in the chest). Together they cover the whole person. He is not describing a particular illness: the perfect 'it has finished' is the sound of a person who has just seen that everything he could lean on will end.

The KJV's 'faileth' is fair, but it makes a weak English verb out of kalah, which means 'is finished, is used up'. It can also mean 'is consumed with longing': Rashi takes it so and cites Ps 119:81 ('my soul has longed for your salvation'), and Metzudat David reads 'my flesh and my heart long for the LORD'. The ambiguity is probably a gift to the actor, who may play the collapse and the longing together. 'God is the strength of my heart' (KJV) loses the image: tzur is a rock or a cliff, the mountain refuge of the Near East, so 'rock of my heart' is concrete. 'Portion' (cheleq) is the word for the share of land each tribe received, except the Levites, whose 'portion' was the LORD himself (Num 18:20). The speaker, in this one word, takes the Levite's place: he has no estate, and he has no need of one. Note that Elohim here is God, the ordinary word, and the one who is called 'my portion' is the same one the verse before called 'you'.

philological_notes.note: 'To be finished, to come to an end', and also 'to long, to pine'. Rashi reads longing (cf. Ps 119:81); Radak reads failing, with the heart as the living soul; I translate as failing and keep longing as the second layer.

'Rock of my heart': a rock or cliff face, the standard image of a safe refuge. Ibn Ezra reads the sense as strength or firmness and links it with what lasts for ever, as against the heart that wears out.

'My portion, my share': an allotment of land. Elsewhere the Levites are told that the LORD is their portion (Num 18:20, Deut 10:9), so the speaker here claims the Levite's inheritance in God; this is my own reading and not a claim of the commentaries in the packet.

verses.translation_literal: For behold, those far from you perish; you have cut off every one who whores from you.
verses.translation_dramatic: For look: those who keep their distance from you are lost. You silence every one who plays the harlot and leaves you.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the speaker's own trouble, the camera turns outward, and the voice hardens. The verse has a double measure: those who are 'far' (rechoqeikha, an adjective meaning 'your far ones') are contrasted with the 'near' of the next verse (qirvat). Distance and nearness are the two poles of the whole closing section, and the actor should let 'far' sound as cold as 'near' will sound warm.

The KJV's 'go a whoring' is an archaism that still keeps the force, but ASV's 'play the harlot' and BBE's 'have not kept faith' turn the image into a mild one. The Hebrew participle zoneh says 'one who acts as a prostitute', and it is a stock prophetic picture of faithlessness to YHWH (Hos 1–3, Jer 3, Ezek 16), where Israel is the wife who goes after other lovers. The picture is of a covenant spouse, not a fault in morals. Rashi softens it to 'one who is separated from you' and Metzudat Zion explains it as 'turning aside' (sarach), which is the root sense, but the image is more pointed than a simple 'departing'. The verb hitzmatah means 'you have silenced, cut off', the same sound as the verb Metzudat Zion points to in Ps 69:5 (tzamat, 'those who would cut me off'). The first verb is imperfect ('they perish') and the second perfect ('you have cut off'), so the verse reads as a rule that has always held, not a threat.

philological_notes.note: 'One who acts as a prostitute': the covenant image of unfaithfulness to God. Metzudat Zion links it to turning aside (sarach), the word for a woman straying from modesty; Rashi reduces it to separation. 'Whoring' keeps the shock that the later translations remove.
'You have silenced, cut off' (hiphil of tsamat). Metzudat Zion glosses it as cutting off, with the parallel in Ps 69:5.

verses.translation_literal: And I, nearness of God [is] good for me; I have placed in the Lord YHWH my refuge, to recount all your works.
verses.translation_dramatic: But as for me, to be near God is my good. I have made the Lord GOD my shelter, and I will tell of everything you have done.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends in an answer to the verse before. 'And I' (va'ani) stands first, set against the 'far ones', and the whole line is one man's choice: to be near. Play it as the settled warmth of someone who has come in from a storm. The speaker began the psalm in near-collapse (v. 2, 'my feet had almost slipped'), and the last line is the fixed place he reached.

The Hebrew qirvat Elohim li tov is clipped: 'nearness of God, to me, good', with no 'it is' and no 'draw near'. The KJV makes it an action ('to draw near to God') and in effect a duty, where the Hebrew names a state, nearness itself, as the good. The KJV's 'I have put my trust in' also replaces a concrete verb: shatti is 'I have set, I have placed', and the object is 'my refuge' (machsi), a shelter from storm or enemy. 'In the Lord GOD' is odd on the page: the text says adonai YHWH, and the pointing of the divine name here is that of Elohim, so that no reader says 'Adonai Adonai' aloud. The last word, malakhotekha, is 'your works' (from mela'khah, 'work, craft, errand'), and the KJV 'declare' is right in spirit; the note of storytelling is there, since saper means to count and to tell. Radak thinks the speaker wants to study the whole of creation, and Metzudat David that he will busy himself with 'the stories of your works and not the talk of others'. The psalm thus ends with a vow to talk, which is also what a worshipper does in the temple.

philological_notes.note: 'Nearness of God': a noun, not an infinitive. Ibn Ezra explicitly sets it against the 'far ones' of v. 27 ('against those who are far from you'), and calls it 'the true good'.
'I have set, I have placed.' Ibn Ezra notes that the form lacks the root's second taw (the doubled tav is a contraction), like karati in 'and I have cut a covenant'.

'Your works, your errands'. Ibn Ezra derives it from the same root as mal'akh (messenger), as 'the work of God'; Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'work and deed'. Rashi reads 'your missions'. 'Works' fits the verb 'to recount'.
